questions.q: For $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$, is $\mathbf{v} = [1,\ 1]^T$ an eigenvector, and if so with which eigenvalue?
options: No, $A\mathbf{v}$ is rotated off the line
questions.explain: $A\mathbf{v} = [3,\ 3]^T = 3\mathbf{v}$, so $\mathbf{v}$ stays on its line and is scaled by $3$. ($\lambda = 1$ is the other eigenvalue, belonging to $[-1,\ 1]^T$.)

questions.q: Using trace $T = a + d$ and determinant $D = ad - bc$, what are the eigenvalues of $A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$?
questions.explain: $T = 7$, $D = 12 - 2 = 10$, so $\lambda = \frac{7 \pm \sqrt{49 - 40}}{2} = \frac{7 \pm 3}{2} = 5, 2$. The diagonal entries $4, 3$ are eigenvalues only for triangular matrices; $7$ and $10$ are $T$ and $D$ themselves.

questions.q: Which preset in the sandbox has **no real** eigenvector at all?
questions.explain: A pure rotation turns every real direction, so $T^2 - 4D < 0$ and the eigenvalues are complex ($\alpha \pm \beta i$). Shear still has one eigenvector line, Identity has every direction, and Reflection has two.

questions.q: Why must $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$ when solving for eigenvalues?
options: $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ needs a **non-zero** solution $\mathbf{v}$, which exists only if $A - \lambda I$ is singular
Because $A$ itself must be singular to have eigenvectors
Because the determinant of any matrix minus $I$ is zero
questions.explain: If $A - \lambda I$ were invertible, the only solution would be $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$, which is excluded. $A$ itself need not be singular (e.g. the reflection has $\det = -1$).
